fetched_contents.text: A Review on Wine Flavour Profiles Altered by Bottle Aging Abstract The wine flavour profile directly determines the overall quality of wine and changes significantly during bottle aging. Understanding the mechanism of flavour evolution during wine bottle aging is important for controlling wine quality through cellar management. This literature review summarises the changes in volatile compounds and non-volatile compounds that occur during wine bottle aging, discusses chemical reaction mechanisms, and outlines the factors that may affect this evolution. This review aims to provide a deeper understanding of bottle aging management and to identify the current literature gaps for future research. Keywords: wine, aroma, mouth-feel, bottle aging, alteration 1. Introduction The flavour composition of a wine generally includes its aroma, taste, and mouth-feel [1], which are arguably the most important contributors that influence wine quality. In general, wine aroma can be divided into the varietal aroma (the fruit type of the aroma), fermentation aroma (the second type of aroma), and aging aroma (the third type of aroma), according to different sources [2]. The taste is primarily defined by non-volatile compounds [3]. For example, bitterness perception can be suppressed by the presence of sugars or glycerol [3]. Wine mouth-feel is considered “the group of sensations characterised by a tactile response in the mouth” [4], and is affected by the tannin and matrix composition, including ethanol, pH, polysaccharides, and their interactions with oral components [5]. The formation of different flavours occurs during different methods of wine aging. Wines are usually aged in oak barrels, stainless steel tanks, and bottles. Oak barrel aging is linked to micro-oxygenation and the transfer of wood compounds, including ellagitannins, furfurals, and norisoprenoids [6], or compounds produced by the practice of “toasting” or burning barrel wood or wood pieces used in aging, like furans, vanillin (a lignin degradation product), or lactones [7]. Barrel-aged wines have a strong, astringent flavour [7]. Wines aged in stainless steel tanks have lower volatile acidity and a lower Folin–Ciocalteu index, more free sulphur dioxide and total sulphur dioxide, and increased acetates, ethyl esters, and fatty acids compared to those aged in oak [8]. On the other hand, bottle aging not only evolves a more fruity aroma and softer mouth-feel than oak barrel aging [9], but also leads to increased phenolic content compared to aging in steel tanks [10]. This remains a hot topic in the wine-making industry [7,11,12,13,14,15,16,17]. Bottle aging is an important process affecting the flavour of wine maturation. There are three main stages of wine quality development in the bottle aging process: the first stage evolves the wine to the mature stage, where wine taste and aroma are improved. The ripening stage (the second stage) is when the wine has the best sensory quality. As the bottle storage time lengthens, the wine enters the third stage, which often leads to a decline in wine quality [18]. Bottle aging is linked to micro-oxygenation, as mentioned above, which is helpful for red wines to reduce astringency and modify the aroma [19]. However, bottle or oak aging is an undesirable process for some white wines because of lower levels of phenolic compounds (PC) (i.e., anthocyanins) of an antioxidant nature [19,20]. The process of bottle aging involves a series of chemical reactions. The mechanisms of the oxidation reaction [5,21,22,23,24,25,26,27], esterification reaction, and hydrolysis reaction [28,29] during the aging process of wine bottles have been widely studied. Recently, more attention has been paid to the mechanism of the Strecker reaction [30,31,32], the influences of closures [14,33], and the alterations of specific compounds which can affect the flavour of wine [12,34,35,36]. Chemical basis of esterification and hydrolysis in wine

Esterification in wine is the formation of esters from carboxylic acids and alcohols, catalyzed by an acid and driven by the reaction of an alcohol with an acid to create an ester linkage. The evidence explicitly states that Fischer esterification is the acid-catalyzed reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols, with the mechanism being an addition-elimination process [N1-F2]. It also notes that ester hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, where esters are cleaved back into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol through reaction with water and a catalytic amount of strong acid, and that this reaction is part of an equilibrium that can be manipulated by Le Chatelier’s principle [N1-F2]. The same source also explains that ester hydrolysis can be shifted toward carboxylic acid formation by using a large excess of water [N1-F2].

In wine chemistry, the most directly relevant compounds are the carboxylic acids and alcohols that form esters, including volatile compounds such as ethyl esters and other ester derivatives. The review evidence indicates that ester formation in wine is linked to H. uvarum esterase activity, while ester hydrolysis and synthesis are also influenced by microbial and environmental factors [N1-R4]. The sensory context provided by the esters section further notes that many esters have characteristic aromas and flavors, with examples such as octyl ethanoate (orange), propyl ethanoate (pear), 2-methylpropyl propanoate (rum), methyl butanoate (apple), and ethyl butanoate (pineapple) [N1-F2]. These examples show that wine esters are not only chemical intermediates but also contributors to aroma and flavor.

The wine-specific evidence also emphasizes that esters are part of a broader family of carboxylic acid derivatives, and that ester hydrolysis can generate carboxylic acids and alcohols, which are among the key compounds affected by these reactions [N1-F2]. The esterification/hydrolysis mechanism therefore applies to wine compounds such as ethanol, acetic acid, and other volatile alcohols and acids, with esters acting as intermediates that can be formed or broken down during aging [N1-R4][N1-F2]. Overall, esterification forms esters from alcohols and acids, while hydrolysis reverses them back into alcohols and acids, and the most affected wine compounds are the volatile acids, alcohols, and their ester derivatives [N1-R4][N1-F2].

Environmental and winemaking factors shaping the reactions during aging

Temperature, humidity, and oxygen exposure all influence the rate and direction of ester-related reactions during aging. The bottle aging review explicitly states that esterification and hydrolysis reactions are closely related to storage temperature and pH during bottle storage [N2-R1]. The storage conditions review adds that ideal cellaring temperatures are around 13–16 °C or 55–60 °F, and that humidity should be maintained around 70% or 50%–70% relative humidity to preserve wine [N2-R2][N2-R4]. These conditions are important because they indirectly control reaction rates: higher temperatures typically increase reaction rates, while lower temperatures can slow chemical changes [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The Jancis Robinson source also notes that alcohol and acidity decrease slightly over time due to esterification, and that bottling can be called “reductive aging” because oxygen exposure is low during bottling [N6-R3][N5-F1].

Oxygen exposure is especially relevant to hydrolysis and other oxidation-driven reactions. The bottle aging review says that oxygen exposure is low during bottling, but it can still induce oxidation reactions that affect aroma and mouth-feel, including pigment polymerisation, tannin condensation, and hydrolysis, as well as the formation of new aromatic compounds and the degradation of peculiar smells [N5-F1]. The same source also notes that micro-oxygenated environments can convert alcohol into aldehydes such as furfural and trans-2-nonenal, which smell like cooked vegetables and wood [N5-F1]. This suggests that while oxygen exposure is generally lower in bottles than in barrels, it can still drive both oxidative and hydrolytic processes, especially when closures or bottle materials allow some oxygen ingress.

Sulfur dioxide, oak, and bottling practices preserve or drive reactions in different ways. The bottle aging review states that wine aging is done using wood fragments, micro-oxygenation, lees, or physical methods to accelerate aging and improve quality [N5-R2]. It also notes that wines aged in oak barrels have a strong, astringent flavor, while stainless steel-aged wines have lower volatile acidity and higher acetates, ethyl esters, and fatty acids [N5-F1]. This indicates that oak aging can both preserve wine through micro-oxygenation and introduce new compounds that alter the flavor profile, while steel aging may favor different ester and acid profiles [N5-F1]. The winemaking evidence further shows that SO2 management is important in aging wines, with sulfur dioxide affecting aromas and textures [N4-R4]. Overall, sulfur dioxide can preserve wine by inhibiting microbial and oxidative reactions, while oak and bottling practices shape the chemical environment in which esterification and hydrolysis occur [N4-R4][N5-F1].

Aging conditions that favor aroma development versus aroma loss depend on the balance between preservation and transformation. The review states that bottle aging can evolve a more fruity aroma and softer mouth-feel than oak barrel aging [N5-F1], but that bottle aging is also linked to micro-oxygenation, which can reduce astringency and modify aroma [N5-F1]. The same review notes that wine quality generally improves in the first stage of bottle aging, reaches a peak in the ripening stage, and declines in the third stage [N5-F1]. The storage conditions evidence also emphasizes that temperature, light, humidity, location, vibration, and packaging and sealing materials all seriously affect wine development [N5-F1]. This means that cooler, stable, and dry conditions tend to favor slower, more controlled aging and aroma development, while excessive heat, humidity, or vibration can accelerate undesirable reactions and lead to aroma loss [N2-R1][N2-R4][N5-F1]. In short, cooler, lower-oxygen, and well-sealed conditions generally favor aroma development, while higher temperatures or excessive oxygen exposure can favor aroma loss and chemical instability [N2-R1][N5-F1].

Hydrolysis products change aroma character over time. Chemical basis of esterification and hydrolysis in wine

Esterification in wine is the formation of esters from carboxylic acids and alcohols, catalyzed by an acid and driven by the reaction of an alcohol with an acid to create an ester linkage. The evidence explicitly states that Fischer esterification is the acid-catalyzed reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols, with the mechanism being an addition-elimination process [N1-F2]. It also notes that ester hydrolysis is the reverse reaction, where esters are cleaved back into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol through reaction with water and a catalytic amount of strong acid, and that this reaction is part of an equilibrium that can be manipulated by Le Chatelier’s principle [N1-F2]. The same source also explains that ester hydrolysis can be shifted toward carboxylic acid formation by using a large excess of water [N1-F2].

In wine chemistry, the most directly relevant compounds are the carboxylic acids and alcohols that form esters, including volatile compounds such as ethyl esters and other ester derivatives. The review evidence indicates that ester formation in wine is linked to H. uvarum esterase activity, while ester hydrolysis and synthesis are also influenced by microbial and environmental factors [N1-R4]. The sensory context provided by the esters section further notes that many esters have characteristic aromas and flavors, with examples such as octyl ethanoate (orange), propyl ethanoate (pear), 2-methylpropyl propanoate (rum), methyl butanoate (apple), and ethyl butanoate (pineapple) [N1-F2]. These examples show that wine esters are not only chemical intermediates but also contributors to aroma and flavor.

The wine-specific evidence also emphasizes that esters are part of a broader family of carboxylic acid derivatives, and that ester hydrolysis can generate carboxylic acids and alcohols, which are among the key compounds affected by these reactions [N1-F2]. The esterification/hydrolysis mechanism therefore applies to wine compounds such as ethanol, acetic acid, and other volatile alcohols and acids, with esters acting as intermediates that can be formed or broken down during aging [N1-R4][N1-F2]. Overall, esterification forms esters from alcohols and acids, while hydrolysis reverses them back into alcohols and acids, and the most affected wine compounds are the volatile acids, alcohols, and their ester derivatives [N1-R4][N1-F2].

Environmental and winemaking factors shaping the reactions during aging

Temperature, humidity, and oxygen exposure all influence the rate and direction of ester-related reactions during aging. The bottle aging review explicitly states that esterification and hydrolysis reactions are closely related to storage temperature and pH during bottle storage [N2-R1]. The storage conditions review adds that ideal cellaring temperatures are around 13–16 °C or 55–60 °F, and that humidity should be maintained around 70% or 50%–70% relative humidity to preserve wine [N2-R2][N2-R4]. These conditions are important because they indirectly control reaction rates: higher temperatures typically increase reaction rates, while lower temperatures can slow chemical changes [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The Jancis Robinson source also notes that alcohol and acidity decrease slightly over time due to esterification, and that bottling can be called “reductive aging” because oxygen exposure is low during bottling [N6-R3][N5-F1].

Oxygen exposure is especially relevant to hydrolysis and other oxidation-driven reactions. The bottle aging review says that oxygen exposure is low during bottling, but it can still induce oxidation reactions that affect aroma and mouth-feel, including pigment polymerisation, tannin condensation, and hydrolysis, as well as the formation of new aromatic compounds and the degradation of peculiar smells [N5-F1]. The same source also notes that micro-oxygenated environments can convert alcohol into aldehydes such as furfural and trans-2-nonenal, which smell like cooked vegetables and wood [N5-F1]. This suggests that while oxygen exposure is generally lower in bottles than in barrels, it can still drive both oxidative and hydrolytic processes, especially when closures or bottle materials allow some oxygen ingress.

Sulfur dioxide, oak, and bottling practices preserve or drive reactions in different ways. The bottle aging review states that wine aging is done using wood fragments, micro-oxygenation, lees, or physical methods to accelerate aging and improve quality [N5-R2]. It also notes that wines aged in oak barrels have a strong, astringent flavor, while stainless steel-aged wines have lower volatile acidity and higher acetates, ethyl esters, and fatty acids [N5-F1]. This indicates that oak aging can both preserve wine through micro-oxygenation and introduce new compounds that alter the flavor profile, while steel aging may favor different ester and acid profiles [N5-F1]. The winemaking evidence further shows that SO2 management is important in aging wines, with sulfur dioxide affecting aromas and textures [N4-R4]. Overall, sulfur dioxide can preserve wine by inhibiting microbial and oxidative reactions, while oak and bottling practices shape the chemical environment in which esterification and hydrolysis occur [N4-R4][N5-F1].

Aging conditions that favor aroma development versus aroma loss depend on the balance between preservation and transformation. The review states that bottle aging can evolve a more fruity aroma and softer mouth-feel than oak barrel aging [N5-F1], but that bottle aging is also linked to micro-oxygenation, which can reduce astringency and modify aroma [N5-F1]. The same review notes that wine quality generally improves in the first stage of bottle aging, reaches a peak in the ripening stage, and declines in the third stage [N5-F1]. The storage conditions evidence also emphasizes that temperature, light, humidity, location, vibration, and packaging and sealing materials all seriously affect wine development [N5-F1]. This means that cooler, stable, and dry conditions tend to favor slower, more controlled aging and aroma development, while excessive heat, humidity, or vibration can accelerate undesirable reactions and lead to aroma loss [N2-R1][N2-R4][N5-F1]. In short, cooler, lower-oxygen, and well-sealed conditions generally favor aroma development, while higher temperatures or excessive oxygen exposure can favor aroma loss and chemical instability [N2-R1][N5-F1].

Sensory consequences for aroma and mouth-feel

Esters in wine contribute fruity, floral, or solvent-like aromas depending on the specific ester and its source. The ester chemistry source lists several esters with characteristic aromas, including octyl ethanoate (orange), propyl ethanoate (pear), 2-methylpropyl propanoate (rum), methyl butanoate (apple), and ethyl butanoate (pineapple) [N1-F2]. These examples show that wine esters are not just chemical intermediates but are directly responsible for the fruity and aromatic character of wine. The microbial modulation review adds that esters are important for wine aroma and that the enzymes responsible for their hydrolysis and synthesis are also relevant [N3-R2]. This means that ester composition can shape the aroma profile by contributing both pleasant fruit and floral notes.

Hydrolysis products change aroma character over time. The bottle aging review explicitly states that ester concentration decreases with hydrolysis to acetic acid and corresponding alcohol during bottle aging [N5-R1]. It also notes that oxidation reactions can produce new aromatic compounds, while degradation can remove peculiar smells [N5-F1]. In addition, the same review points out that micro-oxygenated environments can convert alcohol into aldehydes such as furfural and trans-2-nonenal, which have cooked-vegetable and wood aromas [N5-F1]. This suggests that hydrolysis and oxidation can shift wine aroma from fresh estery notes toward more cooked, oxidative, or even unpleasant notes, depending on the reaction pathway [N5-R1][N5-F1]. The sensory evidence also indicates that wine aroma includes varietal, fermentation, and aging aroma components, with aging aroma being a key contributor to overall quality [N5-F1].

Mouth-feel changes with alcohol, glycerol, and acid shifts. The mouthfeel review states that mouthfeel is a complex and multidimensional sensory experience and is important for how people perceive flavor and accept food and beverages [N3-R1]. It also notes that mouthfeel subqualities such as astringent sensations are common in wines and that the literature evaluates their mention frequency [N3-R4]. The bottle aging review explains that mouth-feel is considered “the group of sensations characterised by a tactile response in the mouth,” and that it is affected by tannin and matrix composition, including ethanol, pH, polysaccharides, and their interactions with oral components [N5-F1]. The same review states that bottle aging can lead to a softer mouth-feel than oak barrel aging [N5-F1]. The sensory impact of malolactic bacteria review adds that malolactic bacteria can positively impact mouthfeel, though their effect depends on conditions [N3-R5]. 

Taken together, the evidence shows that esters support fruity, floral, or solvent-like aromas [N1-F2][N3-R2], hydrolysis and oxidation can shift aroma toward cooked, oxidative, or less desirable characters [N5-R1][N5-F1], and mouth-feel is shaped by ethanol, pH, polysaccharides, tannins, and other matrix components, with bottle aging often producing a softer mouth-feel [N3-R1][N3-R4][N5-F1]. The evidence is consistent with the idea that wine chemistry changes over time in ways that directly affect how the wine feels in the mouth and how it smells [N5-F1].
